speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for Defence with regard to the rejection of National Service deferment for Mr Benjamin Davis (a) what are the criteria to qualify for deferment; (b) whether the Ministry considers a professional contract with an English Premier League football club a rare achievement for a Singaporean; and (c) whether consideration is given to how Mr Davis can contribute to the soccer scene in Singapore when he returns.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: asked the Minister for Defence what are the criteria for a young outstanding athlete in a team sport to be granted deferment from National Service.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: asked the Minister for Defence whether the Ministry will conduct a study to review its criteria for NS deferment for sporting talent, especially in light of more young Singaporeans showing potential and making their mark in regional and international sports.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister, if you have a statement, we can take that later after the Parliamentary Questions (PQs).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singapore's founding leaders knew the strict conditions that National Service (NS) would impose on its citizens when they passed the National Service (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This was 51 years ago and the Enlistment Act in 1970.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 1984, just as he was about to retire, a reflective Dr Goh Keng Swee acknowledged it plain and simple, "National Service imposes (not only) a great sacrifice of time and money on the young men called up." But Dr Goh followed with the reason why this sacrifice was called for and why NS was crucial to our nation's survival.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I continue, quote, Dr Goh's words, "deep in his heart, the average Singapore Citizen knows the danger he faces are real and not hypothetical, and that there is a need to defend ourselves." The Appellate High Court also brought their minds to bear on our NS policy, just as recently as 2017, last year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This was during an appeal on the sentencing of NS defaulters.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Their written judgment spelt out the reasons why more stringent sentencing benchmarks were justified but those same reasons lie at the heart of what various Members of Parliament (MPs) asked today – Dr Lim Wee Kiak, Mr Darryl David, Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap, and Dr Intan Mokhtar in her Question for Written Answer.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In various forms, they asked these questions: how strict is this requirement for every male to serve his NS when required?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was a landmark decision, presided over by the Chief Justice.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Appellate High Court referred to Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean's Ministerial Statement given in 2006 to this House, when he was Defence Minister.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That Ministerial Statement, coupled with the written judgment of the Appellate High Court, illuminates the fundamentals on which our NS policy is based, that we must not unwittingly weaken lest we undo this nation’s foundations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The judges opined that, "In practical terms, what the three fundamental principles of national security, universality and equity mean is that in order to ensure Singapore's national survival, every male Singaporean must serve NS and at the time he is required to under the (Enlistment) Act, without regard to his personal convenience and considerations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In Court, in every case, each of them gave reasons why he did not enlist as required.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some wanted to complete their university degree first before NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is the core of the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The critical need for a strong defence puts aside personal pursuits and mandates that each liable male performs his NS when required.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is the law our founding leaders and subsequent leaders passed in this House.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We may have forgotten it or diluted it, but the Enlistment Act stands.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The written judgment noted that everyone was asked to do his "fair share". "This entails every citizen who is required to serve NS making sacrifices or postponing individual goals to serve the nation when the nation needs his service".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The sum of it – these arguments spell out in unequivocal terms the NS obligations for every Singaporean male.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, deferment cannot be for the individual, no matter how talented, to pursue his own interests or career.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In other words, because I am so exceptional in talent, I deserve to be deferred.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: No matter how talented, and even if it vicariously brings credit or fame to Singapore because that would be fundamentally wrong and goes against the core principle of equity.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Enlistment Act is blind to talent, personal considerations, personal circumstances.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some Singaporeans have voiced the same opinions over Mr Davis' application.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I assume Members filed these questions as a result of that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The sportsmen who were deferred, knew this because clear expectations were laid out when deferment was given.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We discussed it with the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) on the standards required for their training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They will have to return to serve NS, and if they do not meet the standards agreed upon, deferment will be curtailed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These strict conditions are necessary because even for these individuals who can bring glory to Singapore, there are detractors, who think it is unfair for anyone to be deferred.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr T Ng wrote to MINDEF, “Please be fair to all Singaporean males, who spent years serving NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Every Singaporean male’s career is important from his own point of view.” Disruption for individuals after they are enlisted for NS follows the same principles and is also given only for national reasons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We disrupt medical students to complete their medical studies because we need them to serve as Medical Officers during their NS to take care of their fellow soldiers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is not an entitlement, and once the reasons are no longer valid, the disruption will end.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For example, we previously allowed overseas medical students to disrupt, but this was stopped in 1992, when we could produce enough doctors locally.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You can appeal, but we will just say "no", because we have enough.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Similarly, dental students were not disrupted after 1989, as there was no need for NS Dental Officers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And for transparency, MINDEF publishes a full list of all medical students who are disrupted every year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Having stated the general principles, let me explain why the application by Mr Harvey Davis for his son's deferment was rejected even though MINDEF recognised his son, Mr Ben Davis' achievement in obtaining a senior contract with Fulham Football Club (FC).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF is not privy to the contract signed between them, but we assume this published information is correct and that the father must have his reasons for doing so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The father replied to MCCY, Sport Singapore (SportSG) and Football Association of Singapore (FAS), stating, "We are unable to commit to a date for his return should he be playing professional football in the United Kingdom or Europe.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In addition, it is also a possibility that Ben could be offered a new two-year contract in 2019 after the first year of his pro contract just like he has been offered a new two-year pro contract halfway through his two-year scholarship contract.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Or he could be sent out on loan or sold to another club.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There are a lot of variables all dependent on his development and progression." Third, if he was not granted deferment, the father indicated that Mr Ben Davis would still proceed to sign the contract, and he has done so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The reason given by the father was that his son would only return to fulfil his NS commitment if he is unsuccessful in his professional career.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The father's responses made clear his intent for his son to pursue a professional football career to the fullest.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If Mr Ben Davis will not give up his senior contract, which he is now offered, which provides for an allowance of a few hundred pounds a week, to serve his NS, it is even more unlikely that he will return to serve NS if he subsequently gets offered a contract worth many times more.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if he is not given a further contract with Fulham FC, the father has said that he may find other clubs which his son can be loaned to.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The application by Mr Harvey Davis for his son’s deferment is to further his son’s professional career first and to the longest extent possible.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And you would have read what he said.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singapore and her interests, including his son's NS obligations, are secondary considerations, if at all.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There has been no indication, commitment or plans as to how Mr Ben Davis would help football standards in Singapore, if deferred.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Harvey Davis has urged MINDEF to approve deferment for his son so that it would serve as an inspiration, he tells us, for the 1,000 students registered with his company Junior Soccer School and League Singapore (JSSL Singapore), 500 or so who are local.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For your information, JSSL Singapore is a youth football club and academy business run by Mr Harvey Davis and advertises itself as having links to Fulham FC.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is no commitment to serve Singapore or our national interests.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To grant deferment to Mr Ben Davis to pursue his personal development and professional career would be unfair to the many others who have served their NS dutifully as required, and not at a time of their choosing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It would also erode the basis on which our Courts have upheld the Enlistment Act passed by Parliament and punished those for not fulfilling their NS liabilities but instead pursue their own personal concerns and careers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As a writer, Mr Patrick Tan Siong Kuan, wrote to The Straits Times Forum, "The defence of our country cannot be a matter of serving when it is most convenient.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is a responsibility that every man must take seriously when called upon, regardless of race, family connections or financial status.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It takes personal sacrifice and putting the country before self.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Otherwise, there will be no Singapore tomorrow."  Mr Suresh Nair who wrote to the MINDEF Feedback Unit said this, "If Davis is proud of his red passport, he must do what every Singapore teenager does, to dutifully observe the National Service obligations."  I know it must be difficult for a 17-year-old, Mr Ben Davis, to receive such public attention.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was never MINDEF's intent, but we had to respond to his father’s claims to the media to explain to Members of Parliament and Singaporeans the basis of our decision on this crucial national policy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have dealt with the application by Mr Harvey Davis for his son.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think that was the second thing most Members asked.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: National Service does require sacrifices, certainly personal ones, but performing one’s National Service duties and pursuing national aspirations for sports excellence need not be mutually exclusive.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Many talented sportsmen have served National Service as required and yet, at the same time, raised the level of their own skills and the teams they played with.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All three have completed their National Service as required – Saifullah Akbar, and Ikhsan and Irfan Fandi.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, Saifullah Akbar and Ikhsan Fandi asked to be enlisted early, presumably so that they could complete their NS first to pursue their professional careers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Prior to enlisting, Saifullah played for the Under-16 national team and he was actually spotted by a professional Australian club at age 16 but he went ahead to enlist for NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: During their National Service, Irfan and Ikhsan trained and played for the Under-22 national team during the 2017 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They were supported by the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) and Home Team.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am not a football fan, so these clubs are quite foreign to me, but you would know it, football fans out there.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is a good sign for football in Singapore and talented footballers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Talented footballers, Ben Davis included, can emulate the example of Irfan, Saifullah and Ikhsan to complete their National Service duties as required and also advance their professional football careers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, Saifullah Akbar will finish his National Service today and he is going to try out for a European club.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You may have read his interviews, they asked him, "How did you feel when you were called up for National Service?" He said, "I tried to have a positive attitude.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I told myself that army training will strengthen me.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And now that I have finished NS, I can go on to pursue my dreams".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For him, it was never a choice that he had to make not to fulfil his National Service obligations like everyone else.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He said, "I had to train harder" but he kept a positive attitude.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is the kind of example we want young Singaporeans to emulate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the recent SEA Games in 2015 and 2017, MINDEF supported those competing, whether they were competing individually or as a team.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We adjusted some enlistment dates for National Servicemen, so that they could participate in the Games first and enlist later.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Those who were already enlisted were given time off to train and maintain their peak performance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This includes a member of the Water Polo team who clinched their 27th straight SEA Games Gold last year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We wish all these sportsmen every success and hope that they can continue to do well for Singapore in the Asian Games and beyond.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Beyond these provisions, we have offered disruption to Full-time National Servicemen (NSFs) competing in these games.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But very few have chosen to disrupt, presumably because they are able to train adequately in the SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These many examples show that MINDEF has exercised flexibility towards sportsmen competing in team sports, a question asked by Dr Intan Mokhtar, Mr Muhamad Faisal and others.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we have done so without transgressing the fundamentals of National Service and still maintaining equity for all National Servicemen.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think we all agree that National Service is pivotal and essential to our national security.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, is there a rising trend in terms of application for deferment or disruption for NS with regard to sports excellence over the last few years?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Two, if Ben Davis had given a date to say that he would return, would MINDEF consider his deferment?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because this is crucial to state the fundamentals of our National Service policy and from that, whether deferment or disruption can be given.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, the Courts take it very seriously and I know Members here, too.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Member asked specifically whether there has been a trend in increased applications.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I do not have the figures but I do not think so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: What MINDEF has done is to, on its own, work with MCCY and SportSG to increase flexibility, and I gave some details in terms of adjusting enlistment dates, disruptions, time off.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And the fact that we have fewer people disrupting or taking up the offers to disrupt indicates to me that they probably have weighed what they wanted to do and did not see the need to disrupt.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked a hypothetical question: if someone like Mr Davis had said that they would come back, would it have affected our judgement?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have spent a long time explaining how we decide.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you come back to serve your NS, it is your duty.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But the main considerations are: is there a national interest?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It can never be for personal pursuits, it must be for national interest, first and foremost.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I just wanted to clarify two further points.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, I understand that Ben Davis was called up to play for Singapore but he was never capped, which meant he was never fielded for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But is it correct that all those who, in fact, played for Singapore have found a way to do their National Service duties alongside representing the country?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, even where national athletes are deferred, is it always pegged to representing the country at a specific game, for example, rather than just open-ended?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: By the Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) rules, he has not played for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, he is still free to choose which country he wants to play for.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: FIFA rules are quite interesting, and this is from my understanding; I stand corrected, but you can only choose one country for the rest of your life.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That particular shirt you wear can never be changed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even if you change your citizenship, you can only represent one country.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In that sense, I think they have taken a particular philosophy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The question is: do you peg those deferred?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is a misconception that you can be deferred if you are exceptionally talented.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How do you decide between one who is exceptionally talented versus another with exceptional circumstances?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Someone who is poor who needs to work to support his family because the parents are sick.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From the Court's point of view, they have ruled that personal considerations – put aside.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That has been the basis and I think that is correct.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Now, obviously, you need some talent, exceptional talent, to be able to compete and bring glory to the country.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is never easy, it is not a science.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will consider each case with all the facts and make a decision and tell the public, if not satisfy the majority of National Servicemen, who put aside personal considerations to do their National Service duties.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think we all agree on the critical importance of National Service and the sanctity of serving the country.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a couple of supplementary questions, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First of all, will the Minister or MINDEF be prepared to consider sports that perhaps cannot be so quantitatively assessed?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, should a Singaporean sportsman one day win the Australian Junior Open Tennis Championship and have a real possibility of achieving success on a global stage, thereby playing under the Singapore flag, would we be able to consider something like that?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My second question is, would we be able to consider outstanding achievement in activities other than sports, say, in performing arts or perhaps even in music?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And as I have said, it is not a science and, for the cases that we have deferred, they went on to their development and enlisted either at the same time or very soon after their cohorts were also enlisted.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I know that we have on record somebody who entered university in his teens but completed his university education at the same time that his cohorts went to the army and he went in together with them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, the key considerations are how do we maintain equity for all National Servicemen, and for national interests.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I asked a question on deferment during the Committee of Supply in 2012 and I asked my question in relation to the Olympics because there is this constant reference to a high watermark sporting event before deferment is considered by MINDEF, or at least that is the popular perception.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm that, with the Minister's statement, there is no change in the policy for NS deferment?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question actually is picking up from what Dr Lim Wee Kiak said about a two-year contract.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, if a Singaporean commits to return to performing his NS after his cohort has been called up, let us, say, at the age of 18, and that individual says, "At the age of 20, no matter how this training contract goes, I will come back to serve", would MINDEF allow deferment in that particular case?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If I said so in Parliament, it must be so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, it has not changed over the time that MINDEF has administered this policy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: On the second question, my reply to Dr Lim Wee Kiak is that I really do not want to engage in hypothetical circumstances.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And also he has to serve the purposes for deferment based on our current policy.
